messages.content: A vendor slide shows two bars for our quarterly revenue: Q1 bar reaches 96 and Q2 reaches 99 (in $ thousands). The Q2 bar looks about 50% taller. The y-axis starts at 90. Is the growth really 50%?

No. The bars only *look* 50% apart because the axis starts at 90, so you are seeing the parts above 90: Q1 shows 96 - 90 = 6 units of bar, Q2 shows 99 - 90 = 9 units, and 9 is 50% more than 6.

The actual growth is (99 - 96) / 96 = 3.1%. A bar chart encodes value as length from the baseline, so cutting the baseline to 90 multiplies the visual effect by roughly sixteen while the real change stays at 3%. If the bars started at zero, the two would look nearly identical — which is the honest impression for a 3% change.

My dashboard shows churn as a line dropping from 4.2% to 4.0% over six months, and the line falls across almost the whole height of the panel. The y-axis runs from 3.5% to 4.5%. Our VP called it a 'churn collapse.' Is it?

It is a real improvement but not a collapse. The axis spans only 1.0 percentage point (3.5 to 4.5), so a 0.2-point drop fills 20% of the panel height — the chart spends its whole frame on a narrow band.

In relative terms churn fell 0.2 / 4.2 = 4.8%. That is worth having, but 'collapse' would be something like halving. The fix is not necessarily a zero baseline — line charts show position, not length, so a zoomed axis is defensible — but the panel should be labeled with the axis range and the actual values, and the headline should say 'churn down 0.2 points (about 5% relative)', not borrow drama from the geometry.
An ad platform's report shows two bars for conversion rate: 2.1% last month and 2.4% this month. The second bar is four times taller than the first. The axis starts at 2.0%. What is going on?

The visible bar lengths are measured from the axis floor of 2.0%, not from zero. Last month's bar shows 2.1 - 2.0 = 0.1 of height; this month's shows 2.4 - 2.0 = 0.4. Four times the visible height, from a change of 0.3 percentage points.

The true relative improvement is (2.4 - 2.1) / 2.1 = 14.3% — genuinely good, but it is a 14% gain wearing a 300% costume. Whenever a bar chart's axis does not start at zero, mentally subtract the floor from every value before comparing heights, or better, ask for the chart redrawn from zero.

A slide plots our ad spend ($4k, $5k, $6k, $5.5k, $7k, $8k, Jan to Jun) on the left axis (0 to $10k) and signups (210, 240, 260, 250, 300, 330) on the right axis (0 to 350). The two lines track each other beautifully and the presenter says spend and signups move 'in lockstep.' Should I be convinced?

Not by the picture. With two independent axes, the designer chooses each scale freely, and any two series that both drift upward can be made to overlap almost perfectly by stretching or compressing one axis. Here the right axis (0-350) was picked so the signup line sits right on top of the spend line.

The honest check is numerical: signups per $1k of spend are 52.5, 48, 43.3, 45.5, 42.9, 41.3 — efficiency is actually *falling* about 21% across the period even as both totals rise. The lockstep look hides the one thing you would want to know. Ask for the ratio series, or for both series indexed to January = 100 on a single axis.

Our status page slide has website visits on the left axis (0 to 50,000) and server errors on the right axis (0 to 500). The lines cross in March and the presenter says 'errors overtook visits in March, proving the outage drove users away.' Visits in March were 41,000 and errors were 390. What is wrong?

Almost everything. 390 errors did not 'overtake' 41,000 visits — the crossing is an artifact of two unrelated scales sharing one panel. Errors are about 0.95% of visits (390 / 41,000), and a crossing point between lines measured in different units has no meaning at all; move either axis and the crossing moves to a different month.

The claim also leaps from a picture to causation. To argue the outage cost visits you would need visits per day (or hour) around the outage window compared with a normal baseline, not a line-crossing on a dual-axis chart. Treat any dual-axis crossing story as decoration until someone shows you a rate on a single scale.

A news graphic shows unemployment rising from 5% to 7% over two years, but the line slopes *downward* across the page and the headline says 'Joblessness keeps falling.' Values printed on the line are 5.0, 5.6, 6.1, 6.8, 7.0. How can the line fall while the numbers rise?

The y-axis is inverted: 8% is at the bottom and 4% is at the top, so higher values are drawn lower on the page. The data rose steadily from 5.0% to 7.0% — a 2-point increase, or 40% relatively — but your eye reads slope direction, not labels, and the slope says 'down.'

Inverted axes occasionally have a legitimate use (golf scores, race times, 'lower is better' metrics where a designer wants 'good' to be up). But when the inversion is not announced in the title, the chart is arguing the opposite of its own data. First check on any surprising chart: read the axis labels top to bottom before you read the line.

A chart from our facilities team shows average office rent per square foot for four cities as bars: $46, $52, $58, $61. The axis starts at $40 and the $61 bar looks twice as tall as the $46 bar. The caption says 'City D costs double City A.' True?

False. Above the $40 floor, the visible lengths are 6, 12, 18, and 21 — so the $52 bar does look twice the $46 bar's visible stump, and $61 shows 21 against $46's 6, three and a half times. But the real ratio is 61 / 46 = 1.33. City D costs about a third more, not double (and the caption does not even match its own visual trick).

This is the standard truncated-bar illusion: ratios of visible lengths equal ratios of (value - floor), not ratios of values. Any caption using words like 'double' or 'half' on a chart whose axis starts above zero should be recomputed from the printed numbers before it is repeated.

An epidemiology chart in a report plots daily cases of 100, 1,000, 10,000, 100,000 on four consecutive days as points at equal vertical spacing, connected by what looks like a straight line. A colleague says 'growth is steady and linear.' The y-axis has no label I can find. What should I tell him?

The equal spacing is the tell: 100 to 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000 can only sit at equal intervals on a logarithmic axis, where each step up is a multiplication by 10. The growth is not linear at all — cases are multiplying tenfold per day, the most explosive pattern on the page.

On a log axis, a straight line means constant *percentage* growth, and equal distances mean equal ratios, not equal differences. That is a legitimate and useful way to plot explosive data, but only if the axis is labeled and the reader knows the rule. Unlabeled, it converts a ten-thousand-fold increase into a calm-looking ramp. Tell your colleague the chart says the opposite of what he concluded.

Our finance deck plots monthly revenue of $12k, $120k, $1.2M across three years of a log-scale chart, and a board member complains the chart 'makes our growth look flat at the end.' The points for year 2 to year 3 rise by the same vertical distance as year 1 to year 2. Is the chart lying?

No — the board member is reading a log chart with linear eyes. Each year revenue multiplied by 10 (12k to 120k to 1.2M), and on a log axis equal *ratios* get equal distances, so two tenfold jumps correctly draw as two equal steps. The growth rate is constant at 10x per year; nothing flattened.

What did change is the absolute increment: +$108k in the first step versus +$1.08M in the second. A log chart shows the first story and hides the second. Neither is the lie; they answer different questions. If the board cares about dollars added, plot the linear version; if it cares about growth rate, keep the log and label it 'each gridline = 10x' so nobody has to guess.

A colleague insists 'you can never truncate an axis, it's always lying.' But our stock dashboard shows a line chart of share price between $412 and $438 with the axis running $400 to $450, and nobody feels deceived. Who is right?

Both, depending on chart type. The rule that matters is how the chart encodes value. A **bar** chart encodes value as length from the baseline, so a baseline above zero directly falsifies the comparison — that truncation is effectively always misleading. A **line** chart encodes value as position against a scale, like a thermometer; nobody demands a weather chart start at absolute zero.

Your stock line is fine: the axis is labeled, the range ($400-$450) is printed, and readers judge position, not bar length. The honest practice for line charts is to label the range clearly and avoid breathless headlines the zoom does not support. Save your colleague's rule for bars, where it is nearly absolute.

A quality report shows defect rate going from 0.8% to 2.4% year over year, drawn as a nearly flat line near the bottom of a chart whose y-axis runs 0% to 100%. The manager says 'as you can see, defects are basically stable.' Are they?

No — the defect rate tripled (2.4 / 0.8 = 3.0x, a 200% increase). It only looks flat because the axis spends 100 points of range on a metric that lives between 0 and 3. Any change smaller than about 5 points is invisible at that scale.

This is the mirror image of the truncated-axis trick: instead of zooming to exaggerate, you zoom *out* to erase. The right frame for a rate that lives in the low single digits is an axis like 0-4% (for a line chart, with the range labeled), which would show the tripling plainly. When a chart's axis range is fifty times wider than the data's range, ask why.

A sales deck shows a line chart titled 'Sales in decline': it starts in March at 520 units and ends in December at 480, with the headline 'down 8% this year.' I happen to know January was 380 and February was 450. Is the headline fair?

The arithmetic inside the window is right — (480 - 520) / 520 = -7.7%, about -8% — but the window is doing the arguing. March was the year's peak. Across the full year, sales went from 380 in January to 480 in December, which is +26.3%.

Both statements are 'true'; the chart author chose the start point that flips the sign of the story. The defense is a habit: whenever a trend claim surprises you, ask what the series looks like one window wider on each side, and whether the start point is a natural boundary (year start, product launch) or a convenient spike. Peaks and troughs make excellent liars because every number after them is honest.
A survey slide shows approval bars: Candidate A 52%, Candidate B 46%. The axis starts at 40%, and A's bar looks twice as tall as B's. The presenter says 'A is polling double B.' Correct the record.

The visible lengths above the 40% floor are 12 points for A and 6 points for B — that is where 'twice' comes from. The actual figures are 52% versus 46%: a 6-point lead, and a ratio of 52 / 46 = 1.13, so A is polling about 13% higher in relative terms, not 100%.

There is also a second, quieter issue: a 6-point lead on a typical survey may be near the margin of error, which the bar chart's dramatic proportions make it easy to forget. Bars that start at zero would show two nearly equal columns — the correct visual for a close race — and the caption should report the point gap and the margin of error, not a ratio invented by the axis floor.

A chart plots our support team's average first-response time over a day: 42 minutes in January, 38 minutes in June. The line falls dramatically — the drop covers about a quarter of the panel. The axis runs from 30 to 45 minutes. A manager wants to credit a 'transformation program.' What do you say?

The improvement is real but modest: (42 - 38) / 42 = 9.5% faster. It covers a quarter of the panel only because the panel spans just 15 minutes (30 to 45), so each minute gets exaggerated; on a 0-60 axis the same drop would look like a gentle slope.

Whether a transformation program caused a 9.5% gain is a separate question the chart cannot answer — staffing, ticket mix, and seasonality all move response times. Credit the team for a real ~10% improvement, present the axis honestly with its range labeled, and ask for ticket-volume and mix data before attributing the cause. The chart shows *that* times fell; it is silent on *why*.

A chart of quarterly profit uses a log-scale y-axis with bars: Q1 $10k, Q2 $100k, Q3 $1M. The bars get only modestly taller each quarter, and the presenter says growth is 'steady and sustainable.' Something feels off. What is it?

Two problems. First, the growth is not modest: profit multiplied by 10 each quarter (10k to 100k to 1M). 'Steady' is only true in ratio terms. Second, and worse, bars on a log axis are incoherent: a bar's meaning is its length from zero, but a log scale has no zero — log(0) is undefined, so the bars start from an arbitrary floor (here presumably $1 or $1k) and their lengths encode nothing at all.

If you want to show multiplicative growth, use points or a line on a clearly labeled log axis. If you want bars, use a linear axis and let the Q3 bar tower — because it did. A log-scale bar chart combines the worst of both: it borrows the bar's air of concreteness while destroying the thing bars measure.

A consultant's chart shows five years of our energy costs with x-axis points evenly spaced, labeled 2020, 2021, 2023, 2026, 2031 (these are a baseline year plus 1-, 3-, 6-, and 11-year projections). The line rises gently and evenly. Actual costs: 100, 104, 115, 140, 210 (indexed). What's misleading?

The x-axis treats unequal time gaps as equal steps. The five points are spaced as if each were one year apart, so the rise from 140 to 210 — a 50% jump over five years (2031 vs 2026) — gets the same horizontal room as the rise from 100 to 104 over one year. Slopes on this chart are meaningless: steepness no longer corresponds to rate of change per year.

Plotted on a true time axis, the points would bunch at the left and stretch to 2031, and the eye would correctly read 'slow now, steep later.' Whenever x positions are evenly spaced, check whether the x values are. Even spacing is a claim that the intervals are equal, and here that claim is false.

Two lines on one chart: monthly temperature (30, 45, 60, 75 °F, Jan-Apr) on the left axis (0-100) and pool chemical sales ($5k, $9k, $16k, $24k) on the right axis (0-$25k). The lines lie almost on top of each other and the deck says 'sales track temperature perfectly.' A second version of the same slide, right axis 0-$100k, shows the sales line nearly flat along the bottom. Same data. Which slide is true?

Both pictures are 'accurate' and neither proves the claim, which is exactly the problem with dual axes: the vertical relationship between the lines is chosen by whoever sets the scales. On the 0-$25k axis the lines embrace; on the 0-$100k axis they ignore each other.

The underlying relationship is real here — sales do rise with temperature — but the way to show it is a scatter plot (temperature on x, sales on y, one point per month) or a computed ratio: sales per degree are 167, 200, 267, 320 dollars, which actually shows sales growing *faster* than temperature. A chart whose conclusion flips when you rescale an axis has no conclusion; it has a setting.

A hospital's public dashboard shows a bar chart of average ER wait by hospital: ours 34 min, rival 38 min, with the y-axis starting at 30. Our bar looks less than half the rival's. Marketing wants to advertise 'less than half the wait.' Stop them — with numbers.

Visible lengths above the 30-minute floor: ours 34 - 30 = 4 units, rival 38 - 30 = 8 units — hence 'half.' The real comparison is 34 vs 38 minutes: we are 4 minutes faster, which is (38 - 34) / 38 = 10.5% less waiting, not 50%+.

Advertising 'less than half the wait' would be false in a way a regulator can measure, because wait time is a ratio-scale quantity with a real zero and the claim is about the ratio. The honest ad is 'average ER wait 34 minutes — 4 minutes faster than the regional rival,' or simply publish both numbers. If a claim only survives on a truncated axis, it does not survive.

A chart titled 'Engagement skyrockets' shows a line for daily comments: Mon 1,020, Tue 1,035, Wed 1,028, Thu 1,050, Fri 1,061. The line climbs steeply across a tall panel; the y-axis runs 1,000 to 1,070. Skyrocketing?

The total rise is 1,020 to 1,061 = +4.0% across the week, with a dip on Wednesday the steep slope hides. The axis spends its entire 70-point range on a series whose values hover just above 1,000, so a 41-comment change fills most of the panel.

Zoomed axes on line charts are legal but the title has to live within what the zoom shows: 'comments up 4% this week, to about 1,060 a day' is the same data with its clothes on. A useful reflex: read the first and last values off any dramatic line chart and compute the percent change yourself before reading the headline. It takes ten seconds and deflates most skyrockets.

A government chart plots 'cases per 100,000 residents' with the y-axis inverted — the largest value, 300, sits at the bottom and 0 at the top — 'so that improvement reads as up.' Our region, at 240 per 100k, appears low on the page; the best region, at 90, appears near the top. A reader concludes our region is 'near the bottom of the table, so among the worst.' Is the reader right, and what did the chart do?

The reader is wrong about the ranking and the chart invited the error. On this inverted axis, position is reversed: high on the page means *low* value. Our region at 240 per 100k is drawn low because its value is large — and 240 is in fact bad, three times the best region's 90... but the reader reached 'among the worst' by reading position as rank, and several regions between 240 and 300 are worse still. Nothing on the chart can be read by instinct; every value must be looked up numerically.

Inverted axes for 'lower is better' metrics are a recurring temptation, and they fail the same way every time: the reader's first, fastest interpretation — up means more — is wrong on every point. The honest design plots the rate normally (up = more cases) and lets the headline carry the judgment, or plots 'cases avoided per 100k' if an up-is-good direction is truly needed. When you must read an inverted chart, cover the picture and read only the labels.

A startup's pitch deck shows a bar chart of users: 2023 bar to 800k, 2024 bar to 950k. The 2024 bar looks about 20% taller, which matches. But the y-axis starts at 0 and something still feels staged. Then I notice the 2024 bar is also about 20% wider. Why does that matter?

Because area is what the eye actually compares. If height grows 20% and width also grows 20%, the bar's area grows by 1.2 x 1.2 = 1.44 — a 44% visual increase for an 18.75% real one ((950 - 800) / 800). Variable-width bars quietly square the message.

Bars in a chart must share one width so that area stays proportional to height. The same trick appears with icons and 3D objects that scale in every dimension: a 'twice as big' money bag drawn twice as tall *and* twice as wide reads as four times the money. When a graphic's objects grow in two dimensions, ask which single dimension carries the number — and whether the other one is freelancing.

A chart shows our two products' market share over 8 quarters as lines on a dual-axis plot — Product A (left axis, 0-60%) rising 22% to 31%, Product B (right axis, 0-10%) rising 3% to 6%. The lines converge and the deck says 'B is catching up to A.' Is it?

In percentage points, no: A gained 9 points (22 to 31) while B gained 3 points (3 to 6), so the gap *widened* from 19 points to 25 points. The convergence is manufactured by giving B an axis six times more zoomed (0-10 vs 0-60), so each of B's points gets six times the vertical travel of A's.

There is a sense in which B grew faster — it doubled (3 to 6 is +100%) while A grew 41% relatively — and if that is the claim, the honest chart plots both on one axis or indexes both to their starting values. 'Catching up' in share means closing the point gap, and that is the one thing that did not happen. Dual axes let a deck assert a relationship that no single scale would support.
A market-share pie chart has 14 slices: 12, 11, 11, 10, 10, 9, 9, 8, 6, 5, 4, 3, 1, 1 percent. The presenter says 'as the pie clearly shows, the leader is pulling away.' Does it show that?

It shows almost nothing, which is the problem. The leader has 12% and the runner-up 11% — a 1-point gap. In angle terms that is 43.2 degrees versus 39.6 degrees, a difference no eye can detect, especially with 14 slices in similar colors and labels in a legend across the page.

Pie charts ask readers to compare angles and areas, the two judgments people are worst at, and they get worse with every added slice and every near-tie. The same data as a sorted horizontal bar chart would show the truth instantly: a crowded field bunched between 8% and 12%, with a long tail — a story about fragmentation, not a runaway leader. 'Clearly shows' is doing all the work in that sentence.

A survey asked users 'which features do you use? (select all that apply)' and got: Search 68%, Filters 54%, Saved items 47%, Alerts 31%. The results were published as a pie chart with four slices. What's wrong?

The four numbers sum to 200%, not 100%, because each respondent could pick several features. A pie chart is a picture of parts of a single whole — its slices must exhaust one pie and exclude each other. Drawing these as slices silently claims that 68% + 54% + 47% + 31% partitions the users, which would mean, absurdly, that the 'Alerts' slice is a separate group of people from the 'Search' slice.

The honest graphic is a simple bar chart of four percentages, which makes no whole-pie promise. Rule of thumb: if the percentages can sum to anything other than 100, a pie is not just ugly, it is false.

Two pie charts side by side show our revenue mix. 2023 (total $2M): Product X is a quarter of the pie. 2024 (total $5M): Product X is still a quarter of the pie. A manager concludes 'X hasn't grown.' Hasn't it?

It has grown 150%. A quarter of $2M is $500k; a quarter of $5M is $1.25M. X's revenue went from $0.5M to $1.25M — an extra $750k — while its *share* stayed flat at 25%.

Pies normalize away the total: every pie is exactly 100% by construction, so two pies can never show growth, only redistribution. Side-by-side pies are one of the most common ways real growth (or real decline) disappears from a report. If totals matter, show them: stacked bars with dollar heights, or a table with both share and absolute values. A pie answers 'what fraction?' and refuses every other question.

A report plots customer satisfaction by department — HR 3.9, Sales 4.2, Operations 3.6, Legal 4.0, Support 3.8 (out of 5) — as a line chart, and the line zigzags dramatically. The write-up says 'satisfaction plunged at Operations, then recovered at Legal.' What's the category error?

Departments are categories, not a sequence. A line asserts that between Operations and Legal there is a continuum you pass through — that 'plunging' and 'recovering' happened along the way. But the x-axis order is arbitrary (alphabetical here, most likely); reorder the departments and the same data 'plunges' somewhere else or not at all.

Lines are for ordered quantities: time, temperature, dose. Categories get bars, which make no continuity promise and invite comparison rather than narrative. The zigzag shape is an artifact of the sort order, and every verb in that write-up — plunged, recovered — was generated by the chart type, not the data.
Someone charted our monthly signups for Jan-Jun (900, 1,100, 1,050, 1,300, 1,250, 1,500) as a pie chart with six slices. It looks fine to me — each month is a slice. Why did our analyst object?

Because a pie asserts that the slices are shares of a meaningful whole, and 'the sum of six months of signups' (7,100) is not a whole anyone cares about — June's slice is not '21% of the half-year' in any decision-relevant sense, and the pie throws away the one thing monthly data is for: the order and the trend.

As a line or column chart, the same numbers tell their story at a glance: growth from 900 to 1,500 (+67%), with dips in March and May. As a pie, you get six similar wedges and a legend. Chart types are claims about structure: pie claims part-to-whole, line claims sequence. Picking the wrong one does not just look odd, it deletes information.

A 3D bar chart in a vendor deck shows three products' scores: the bars are labeled 30, 45, and 60, but the middle bar (45) looks noticeably taller than the 60 bar behind it. The vendor says 'trust the labels.' Should the chart survive review?

The labels may be accurate, but the chart should not survive. In a 3D rendering, a bar's apparent height depends on its depth position and the viewing angle: perspective makes nearer bars loom larger, the tops are parallelograms so 'the top of the bar' is ambiguous, and back bars are partly hidden behind front ones. Your eye compares the geometry, gets 45 > 60, and the labels arrive too late to fix the impression.

3D adds no information to a bar chart — every value is one number — it only adds distortion. The professional standard is flat bars on a shared baseline. When a deck reaches for 3D, ask what the flat version would look like; occasionally the answer is 'less impressive,' which is the point of the 3D.

A chart shows website traffic by source as a stacked area chart over 12 months: Organic, Social, Paid, Referral layers stacked on top of each other. Total traffic was flat all year (about 100k/month), but the Social layer (the second one up) looks like it wobbles wildly. Social's actual numbers were steady: 18k-20k every month. Why does it look unstable?

In a stacked area chart, only the bottom layer has a fixed baseline. Every layer above it rides on the cumulative total of the layers below, so Social's top *and bottom* edges both move whenever Organic (below it) moves — Social can look like it surges and crashes while its own thickness, the only thing that represents it, barely changes. Readers naturally track the top edge of a band, and that edge belongs to Organic + Social combined.

If the question is 'how did each source trend?', use separate lines or small multiples, where every series gets the same baseline. Stacked areas answer exactly one question well — 'how is the total composed right now?' — and quietly sabotage the per-series question.

A bubble chart compares four cities' startup funding: A $50M, B $100M, C $200M, D $400M. The bubbles' *radii* are proportional to funding, so D's bubble has 8x the radius of A's. A reader says D looks 'way more than 8 times' A. Are they right, and what's the correct encoding?

The reader is right. Area grows with the square of radius: D's radius is 8x A's, so its area is 64x A's — for a funding ratio of only 8x (400 / 50). The chart shouts 64 where the data says 8.

The correct encoding makes *area* proportional to value: radius should scale with the square root of the value. For an 8x value ratio, the radius ratio should be sqrt(8) = 2.83. Even done correctly, area is a weak encoding — people underestimate area differences — so bubbles are best for spotting rough patterns, with values labeled. When a bubble chart feels dramatic, check whether radius or area carries the number; radius-encoded bubbles always exaggerate, by squaring.

A stacked bar chart shows profit by quarter for two divisions, but Division B lost money in Q2 (-$40k) while Division A made $90k. In the stack, B's segment in Q2 is drawn *below* the axis while A's sits above, and the total bar height reads as $130k tall overall. The CFO's summary says 'combined Q2 profit $130k.' Fix it.

Combined Q2 profit is 90 + (-40) = $50k, not $130k. The $130k comes from adding the *lengths* of the two segments (90 above the line, 40 below it), which is what a stacked bar invites you to do — but stacking presumes all parts push the same direction from one baseline. A negative segment breaks the geometry: the column spans from -40 to +90, and its total visual height (130) is the range, not the sum.

Mixed positive/negative contributions should not be stacked. Use grouped bars, or a waterfall chart that walks from 0 up 90, down 40, landing at 50 — the waterfall's landing point *is* the answer, which is what the CFO needed.

A slide shows a donut chart of our budget: the slices are labeled 40%, 35%, 25% and the big number in the donut's hole says 'Total: $1.2M.' The three categories are actually $400k, $350k, and $250k. Spot the inconsistency.

The percentages describe a $1.0M budget, not $1.2M: $400k + $350k + $250k = $1,000k, and indeed 400/1000 = 40%, 350/1000 = 35%, 250/1000 = 25%. Against the printed $1.2M total, the shares would be 33.3%, 29.2%, and 20.8% — summing to only 83.3%, leaving $200k unaccounted for.

Either the total in the hole is wrong or a $200k category is missing from the slices. Donut charts make this easy to miss because the center number and the ring are produced by different fields in most dashboard tools, and nobody re-adds them. The check takes five seconds: the slices' values must sum to the total the graphic claims, and the percentages must be those values divided by that total.

An infographic shows our growth with rows of money-bag icons: 2022 has 2 bags for $200k revenue, 2023 has 3 bags for $300k, 2024 has 4 bags — but the 2024 bags are drawn about twice as tall as the earlier ones, for $400k. A designer says 'same count logic, just bolder.' What's the distortion?

Pictograms only work if every icon is identical, so count alone carries the value. Here 2024 has 4 bags (which correctly says $400k at $100k per bag) but each bag is drawn twice as tall and roughly twice as wide — about 4x the area per bag. The 2024 row therefore presents something like 16x the ink of the 2022 row for 2x the revenue.

It is the scaling trap from the pitch-deck bars again: growing a symbol in two dimensions squares (or worse) its visual weight. Icons in a pictogram must be copy-pasted, never resized. If the design needs emphasis, use color — area must stay boring.

A line chart shows average temperature by month for two cities, but the analyst plotted the months in the order Jan, Feb, Mar... for City 1 and then appended City 2's months continuing along the same x-axis, so the line runs 24 points long with a sharp drop in the middle where City 2 starts. A reader asks 'why did it get so cold in month 13?' What went wrong?

There is no month 13 — the x-axis silently switched cities halfway. The single continuous line asserts one series evolving over 24 periods; the cliff in the middle is just the seam between two different datasets (City 1's December to City 2's January), and it is the most dramatic feature on the chart while meaning nothing.

Two series need two lines (or two panels), each labeled, over the same 12-month axis. Concatenating series end-to-end is a data-shaping error that line charts are uniquely good at hiding, because the line dutifully connects whatever it is fed — including the join between unrelated things. A line connecting two points is a claim that the path between them exists.

A report uses a pie chart to show the *change* in each region's sales this year: Northeast +$50k, South +$30k, Midwest -$20k, West +$40k. The Midwest slice is drawn as a normal wedge. What's conceptually broken?

A pie is built from shares of a positive total. Changes can be negative, and there is no wedge for -$20k: a slice with negative angle does not exist, so the tool either dropped the sign (drawing Midwest as +20 of a 140 total) or dropped the region. Either way the graphic asserts Midwest *contributed* a positive slice of something.

Changes get bars: diverging bars from a zero line show +50, +30, -20, +40 with direction intact, and the net change (+$100k) is computable from them. The deeper rule: a chart type encodes assumptions — pie assumes parts of a positive whole, diverging bars assume signed deviations. When the data violates the assumption, the chart does not complain; it just lies quietly.

A funnel graphic in our growth deck shows: Visits 100,000 → Signups 40,000 → Trials 30,000 → Paid 25,000, drawn as four centered trapezoids. But the widths look like 100%, 75%, 55%, 50% rather than matching the numbers. The designer says funnels are 'illustrative.' Your response?

Then the illustration contradicts the data. The real stage-to-stage picture: signups are 40% of visits, trials are 75% of signups, paid are 83% of trials, and overall conversion is 25%. The drawn widths (75%, 55%, 50% of the top) match none of these — the first drawn drop looks gentle (100 to 75) when the actual first drop is the brutal one (100 to 40).

Funnels already have one honest job: showing where the big leak is. Here it is visit-to-signup, and the drawing hides exactly that. If widths are not to scale, the funnel is a list wearing a costume — just publish the four numbers and the three conversion rates, which is more informative and takes less space.

A chart plots our product's rating distribution as a smooth line: 1-star 5%, 2-star 8%, 3-star 17%, 4-star 30%, 5-star 40%. The line makes it look like a continuous wave cresting at 5. A statistician winces. Why?

Star ratings are five discrete buckets; nothing exists between 3 and 4 stars, but the smooth curve draws values there anyway and, worse, its *area under the curve* and slopes imply a continuous density that was never measured. The smoothing also rounds off the distribution's real shape — the dip at 2 stars and the jump at 5 — which is the interesting part (a polarized product with a happy majority).

Bars preserve the discreteness: five columns, each height a measured share, summing to 100%. Lines and curves are for quantities that actually vary continuously. The general test: could the x-axis hold a value between two neighbors (3.5 stars, in a sense the average can, but no review can)? If not, do not connect the dots.

A dual-line chart of our churn (left axis, %) and revenue (right axis, $) is replaced by a designer with a single chart: both series indexed to 100 in January. Churn went 100 → 118 (index) while revenue went 100 → 106. The CMO complains the new chart 'hides the real levels — churn is 3.9%, not 118 of anything.' Is the redesign defensible?

Yes — it trades one kind of information for another, openly. The indexed chart cannot tell you churn is 3.9% (it must be labeled in the caption), but it does the one thing the dual-axis chart only pretended to do: put both series' *growth rates* on a single, honest scale, where 118 vs 106 genuinely means churn grew about three times faster than revenue ((18% vs 6%)).

Every chart hides something; the question is whether what it hides is what it claims to show. Dual axes claim comparability they do not have; indexing claims growth comparison and delivers it, at the stated cost of levels. The mature format is the indexed chart plus a small table of actual levels — picture for the pattern, numbers for the magnitudes.

A 'waterfall' slide in a board deck actually isn't: it shows five free-standing bars for revenue components — New sales $500k, Upsells $200k, Churn -$150k, Downgrades -$50k, Net $500k — all starting from zero, and a board member asks why the components don't add to the net bar. Do they?

They do: 500 + 200 - 150 - 50 = 500. The net is $500k and the arithmetic is fine. The confusion is presentational: drawn as independent bars from zero, the negative bars hang below the axis and nothing visually accumulates, so the eye cannot verify the sum — the one job a waterfall exists to do.

In a true waterfall, each bar starts where the previous ended: 0 → 500 (new) → 700 (upsells) → 550 (churn) → 500 (downgrades) → final total bar at 500. The floating steps make the bridge from components to total *visible*, and a wrong number becomes obvious because the last step would not land on the total. If the audience has to do mental arithmetic to check your chart, the chart has failed at its only task.

A marketing graphic shows a world map with countries colored by our app's total downloads: India darkest, then Brazil, then the US, then Germany lightest. The headline: 'India loves us most.' Downloads: India 2.1M (population 1.4B), Brazil 1.5M (216M), US 1.2M (335M), Germany 0.6M (84M). Re-rank honestly.

By downloads per million residents: India 2.1M / 1,400 = 1,500 per million; Brazil 1.5M / 216 = about 6,900 per million; US 1.2M / 335 = about 3,600 per million; Germany 0.6M / 84 = about 7,100 per million. The honest ranking is Germany and Brazil at the top (roughly 7,000 per million each), then the US, with India *last* at 1,500 — the map's hero is the weakest market per capita.

Raw-count maps mostly redraw the population map: big countries are dark for almost every metric. Color by a rate (per capita, per user, per store) and the story can reverse entirely, as it does here. 'Loves us most' is a claim about intensity, and intensity is always a ratio.

A slide shows two area charts of the same support-ticket data. Version 1 (filled area under a line of tickets per day, 200-260 range) is described as 'tickets surging.' Version 2 plots the same data as a plain line. The numbers are identical. Why does the area version feel more alarming?

Because the filled area gives the series *mass*: the eye integrates the whole colored region, so a rise from 200 to 260 (+30%) reads as a large growing body rather than a line moving up a scale. The fill also anchors attention on the area between the line and zero — most of which is the constant baseline of ~200 tickets that never changed.

Area charts are honest for quantities where the accumulated total matters (cumulative rainfall, inventory over time). For a rate or level, the fill is pure emphasis. When a chart of ordinary operational data feels physically heavy, check whether the weight is coming from ink rather than information — and ask for the line version to see the change at its true size.

Our HR dashboard shows headcount by office as a pie: Austin 45, Denver 45, Chicago 90, Remote 120 (total 300). A new hire looking at the pie says 'Remote looks like about a third.' It's 40%. Why the underestimate, and is the pie at fault?

Remote is 120 / 300 = 40%, a 144-degree slice. People systematically underestimate large slices' shares because angle and area judgment compresses differences — 40% vs the 30% slices (108 degrees) for Chicago is a 36-degree difference that reads as 'a bit bigger.' The new hire's 'about a third' (33%) is the classic pie-reading error: errors of 5-10 points are normal even with few slices.

With only four categories this pie is legal but still lossy. A bar chart — 120, 90, 45, 45 on a shared scale — makes the 40% and the exact tie between Austin and Denver unmissable. Pies survive in dashboards mostly by tradition; wherever a decision depends on the number, bars deliver it with less squinting.

Our growth dashboard shows 'monthly active users' jumping from 48,000 in March to 61,000 in April — a 27% leap that got celebrated in all-hands. Buried in the release notes: in April the definition changed from 'logged in within 30 days' to 'any event within 30 days, including email opens.' How much of the leap is real?

None of it is measurable from this chart, and that is the point. The arithmetic (61,000 - 48,000) / 48,000 = 27.1% compares two different quantities wearing one label. Email opens sweep in thousands of people who never touched the product, so some unknown share of the +13,000 is definitional, and the real change could be positive, flat, or negative — the spliced series cannot say.

The correct handling: recompute the old months under the new definition (or the new month under the old), publish both series across the seam, and mark the break on the chart. A KPI whose definition changes must be versioned like code. Any trend line that crosses a silent definition change is fiction with good formatting.

Three slides in one deck report three different 'active user' numbers for the same product in the same month: 12,000 (daily actives), 38,000 (weekly), 95,000 (monthly). An investor asks 'so how many active users do you have?' What's the honest answer?

All three, with their windows attached — 'active user' is not a number, it is a number plus a window plus an action definition. 12,000 people use it on a typical day, 38,000 in a typical week, 95,000 in a typical month. The ratios are informative too: DAU/MAU = 12,000 / 95,000 = 12.6%, which says the average monthly user shows up about one day in eight — a casual-use product, not a daily habit.

The dishonesty risk is picking whichever figure suits the audience: 95,000 for investors, 12,000 for capacity planning. Pin the definition wherever the number appears ('MAU = unique users with a session in the trailing 30 days') and never let the bare phrase 'active users' travel alone.

Our API dashboard proudly shows 'average response time: 240 ms.' But the same dashboard lists p95 = 1,900 ms and p99 = 4,200 ms, and we serve about 200,000 requests a day. Support keeps getting 'your API is unusably slow' tickets. Reconcile the average with the tickets.

Both are telling the truth about different populations. The mean of 240 ms is dominated by the huge majority of fast requests. But 5% of 200,000 is 10,000 requests a day slower than 1.9 seconds, and 1% is 2,000 requests a day slower than 4.2 seconds. If a customer's workflow makes 50 API calls, they will hit the slow tail several times a day — their experienced product *is* the tail.

Latency is a distribution, not a number, and the mean is the worst single summary of it because it hides exactly the requests users remember. Dashboards should lead with p50, p95, p99 (and the mean can come along for capacity math). 'Average 240 ms' and '10,000 slow requests a day' are the same system; only one of those sentences explains the tickets.

Finance changed our revenue KPI in July from 'gross bookings' to 'net recognized revenue.' The annual chart now shows Jan-Jun averaging about $10.2M/month (bookings) and Jul-Dec about $8.4M/month (recognized), with a cliff in July that the sales team is being blamed for. Bookings actually grew steadily all year. What happened?

The chart splices two different metrics at July and reads the seam as an event. Bookings and recognized revenue differ structurally — recognized excludes cancellations, refunds, and revenue deferred to future periods — so a level shift of roughly (10.2 - 8.4) / 10.2 = 17.6% at the switch is expected even with identical business performance.

Nothing fell in July; the ruler changed. The repair: restate the whole year on the new definition (finance has the data), or plot both definitions as separate lines with the old one ending in June, and annotate the seam. Blaming a team for a definitional cliff is the most expensive version of this error, because the chart looks authoritative while comparing unlike quantities.

Our community app's dashboard leads with 'Total registered users: 1,200,000' — a number that has risen every single month for three years. Meanwhile weekly active users quietly fell from 41,000 to 34,000 this year. Why does the headline metric never go down, and why is that a problem?

Because it is a cumulative counter: registrations only add, and accounts are never subtracted, so the line is mathematically incapable of falling. It measures the integral of all past marketing, not the current health of anything. A product could lose every active user and the headline would still 'grow' by however many signed up and left.

Meanwhile the metric that can move both ways — weekly actives — fell (41,000 - 34,000) / 41,000 = 17.1%, which is the actual story of the year. Vanity metrics share a signature: they are big, cumulative, and always improving. Decision metrics are smaller, windowed, and capable of embarrassing you. A dashboard should lead with a number that is allowed to go down.

A mobile game's dashboard celebrates '500,000 downloads.' The retention panel shows day-30 retention of 2%. The CEO wants to double the ad budget because 'acquisition is working.' Do the math she is skipping.

2% of 500,000 is 10,000 players still present at day 30 — meaning 490,000 of the celebrated downloads are gone within a month. Acquisition is 'working' only at producing downloads; the funnel converts them to retained players at 2%.

Doubling ad spend at the same retention doubles both numbers: 1,000,000 downloads and 980,000 departures. Whether that is good business depends on cost per download versus revenue per retained player — figures the downloads headline cannot express. The dashboard pairs a vanity numerator (downloads) with no denominator discipline. The decision metric is cost per day-30 retained user, and on that metric nothing has been shown to work yet.

Our conversion KPI 'improved' from 3.0% to 5.0% in one month with no product change. The changelog shows the denominator switched from sessions (100,000) to unique users (60,000), with the same 3,000 orders. Explain the 'improvement.'

3,000 / 100,000 sessions = 3.0%; 3,000 / 60,000 users = 5.0%. Same orders, same business — the rate rose 67% because each user averages 1.67 sessions, and counting users instead of sessions shrinks the denominator by that factor.

Neither denominator is 'wrong': per-session conversion suits funnel analysis, per-user suits marketing attribution. But a KPI whose denominator changed is a new KPI, and plotting it as a continuation of the old line manufactures a win. Denominators are part of the metric's identity — the three questions for any rate are numerator, denominator, and window, and a change to any of them restarts the series.

A SaaS dashboard reports 'churn: 5.0%' for the month — we lost 10 of 200 customers. Revenue churn for the same month is 1.5%. The board sees one slide with just '5.0%.' What is each number actually saying, and which belongs on the slide?

Logo churn counts customers: 10 / 200 = 5.0% of accounts left. Revenue churn weights them by money: the 10 who left were small accounts representing only 1.5% of monthly recurring revenue. Both are true; they describe different risks. Logo churn says the product is failing small customers (a future pipeline problem — today's small accounts are tomorrow's large ones); revenue churn says the current income base is comparatively stable.

Showing only 5.0% overstates the immediate financial damage; showing only 1.5% would hide the small-customer problem. Mature dashboards show both, labeled, because each triggers a different response: revenue churn is a finance alarm, logo churn is a product alarm. An unlabeled 'churn' is a number waiting to be misunderstood.

Our CSAT dashboard jumped from 41% to 78% 'satisfied' in one quarter. The survey didn't change, but I learn the definition of 'satisfied' was widened from 'gave 5 out of 5' to 'gave 4 or 5.' The underlying distribution both quarters: 5s = 41%, 4s = 37%, 3s = 12%, 2s = 6%, 1s = 4%. What really happened?

Nothing changed except the ruler. Under the old definition, satisfied = 41% (the 5s). Under the new one, 41 + 37 = 78%. The distribution you quoted is identical, so customer sentiment moved by exactly zero while the KPI rose 37 points.

Top-box (5-only) and top-two-box (4-5) are both legitimate conventions — but they are different metrics with different names, and switching mid-series without restating history manufactures the largest 'improvement' in the dashboard's history out of a definition edit. The giveaway for this pattern: a huge jump in a survey metric with no corresponding movement in behavior metrics (retention, repeat purchase, ticket volume). When one number leaps and its cousins do not move, suspect the definition before celebrating the team.

A status dashboard shows 'average p95 latency across regions: 310 ms' — computed by taking each region's p95 (US 180, EU 260, Asia 490) and averaging them: (180+260+490)/3 = 310. Our SRE lead says this number is meaningless. Why?

Because percentiles do not average. A p95 is a property of a whole distribution — the value below which 95% of observations fall. The mean of three regional p95s is not the p95 of the pooled traffic, and it is not any region's p95 either; it is a number with no population it describes. If Asia carries 60% of traffic, the true global p95 sits much closer to Asia's distribution than 310 suggests; if Asia carries 5%, the opposite.

The correct approach: compute the percentile from the pooled latency histogram (or from stored per-request data), weighted by actual traffic. Percentiles, like ratios, must be recomputed from the underlying counts, never averaged from summaries. Any dashboard cell produced by averaging percentiles (or averaging percentages with different bases) should be treated as decorative.

Our streaming dashboard reports 'engagement: 4.1 billion minutes watched this month, up 12%.' Product quietly enabled autoplay-next-episode and background play in the app this month. As the analyst, what do you flag?

That the metric now counts minutes nobody chose to watch. Autoplay converts one decision ('play episode 1') into hours of 'engagement,' and background play counts minutes when the screen is off. The +12% may be entirely the instrumentation change — the ruler again — with intentional viewing flat or down.

Engagement minutes are a proxy for value only while the playing is deliberate. The fixes: split the metric into user-initiated minutes versus autoplay/background minutes and trend them separately, and restate or annotate the seam. The general law: when a metric can be increased by the team that reports it, by changing what counts rather than what happens, it will be — dashboards need definition changelogs exactly like APIs do.

A hotel chain's dashboard shows 'occupancy: 92%.' I learn the numerator counts rooms *held* (including complimentary holds and out-of-service rooms blocked for maintenance) over total rooms. Paid occupied rooms are 71 of 100 on a typical night. What is the gap between the dashboard and reality?

The dashboard overstates sellable occupancy by 21 points: 92% counts 21 rooms that earn nothing (holds and maintenance blocks) as 'occupied,' while paying guests fill 71%. Revenue per available room — the metric owners actually bank — is computed off the 71, so the 92% flatters operations while the money follows the lower number.

Every KPI embeds a numerator decision, and 'occupied' is doing heavy lifting here. The discipline is to define KPIs in terms of the decision they feed: if the question is 'are we filling the hotel with paying guests?', the numerator is paid room-nights, full stop. When a dashboard number and the bank account disagree, the definition is the first suspect.

Our error-rate KPI reads 0.1%: 900 errors over 900,000 requests. A sister team reports the same system's errors as 3.0%: the same 900 errors over 30,000 user sessions. Both dashboards are 'correct.' Which one should leadership see?

Both are correct arithmetic — 900 / 900,000 = 0.1% per request; 900 / 30,000 = 3.0% per session — but they answer different questions, and leadership usually needs the session one. Per-request error rate describes the *system's* reliability per operation; per-session describes the *user's* chance of hitting an error during a visit: 3% of sessions, about 1 in 33, contain an error. That is the number that predicts complaints.

The 30x gap between the two is purely the denominator (each session makes ~30 requests). Presenting only 0.1% to leadership understates user pain by design. Rates should always travel with their denominator named in the label: 'errors per request' and 'sessions with at least one error' are different metrics, and dashboards that just say 'error rate' are hiding a choice someone made.

A recruiting dashboard shows 'pipeline coverage: 3.2x' — total pipeline value divided by quota. Recruiters assign stage probabilities (10%, 25%, 50%, 80%) to weight deals, but I notice the weighted pipeline uses the probabilities while the 3.2x headline divides *unweighted* pipeline ($9.6M) by quota ($3M). Weighted pipeline is $3.4M. What is the honest coverage?

Weighted coverage is 3.4 / 3.0 = 1.13x — the team has barely more than quota in probability-adjusted pipeline, a thin position, versus the comforting 3.2x on the slide. The headline divides a raw sum (every deal counted at full value, including 10%-stage long shots) by quota and calls the result coverage.

Mixing a weighted concept with an unweighted numerator is a common dashboard bug because both numbers live in the same CRM. The rule: a ratio is only meaningful if numerator and denominator were built under one consistent definition. 3.2x and 1.13x lead to opposite decisions (relax vs. urgently generate pipeline), so this is not pedantry — the mislabeled ratio is the decision.

Our e-commerce dashboard's hero metric is 'Revenue today' — but 'today' resets at midnight UTC while our customers are mostly in US time zones, and the number is compared against 'yesterday' at whatever time someone looks. At 9am Eastern the chart shows today 'down 61%' versus yesterday. Is the store in trouble?

Almost certainly not — the comparison is between a partial day and a complete one. At 9am Eastern, 'today' (UTC) has accumulated 9 hours of a day whose US selling hours have barely started, while 'yesterday' shows its full 24. A -61% reading at that moment is mostly clock arithmetic, and it will 'recover' all day regardless of what the business does.

Time-window definitions are part of the metric. Honest dashboards compare like with like: today-so-far versus the same elapsed window yesterday (and label it 'vs yesterday, same hours'), in the business's own timezone. Any 'today vs yesterday' tile read before the day closes is measuring the time of day, not performance — and teams that panic at it every morning learn to ignore the dashboard entirely, which is its own cost.

A fitness app's dashboard shows 'Workouts completed: up 34% month over month.' The app also shipped an update that auto-logs a workout when the phone detects 10 minutes of walking, where before users logged workouts manually. Old definition count for this month would have been about 8,200; the dashboard shows 11,000. Decompose the 34%.

The definitional share is essentially all of it. (11,000 - 8,200) / 8,200 = 34.1% — matching the headline almost exactly, which means under the old definition, workout volume was flat and the entire 'growth' is the auto-logging change sweeping in walks that were never counted before.

Auto-logging may even be a better metric — walks are exercise — but it is a *new series*, and presenting it as month-over-month growth is false. The dashboard should restart the trend at the change, annotate it, and ideally dual-run both definitions for a month so the seam can be quantified. When a growth number and a definition change arrive in the same month, assume the change explains the growth until someone proves otherwise with a restated series.

Our SaaS 'customers' KPI counts every workspace ever created, including free trials that expired years ago: 14,300 'customers.' Paying accounts are 2,150. Marketing uses 14,300 in a deck; finance uses 2,150. Who is right?

Finance, for any sentence containing the word 'customer.' A workspace created once by a trial user who never paid and never returned is a historical event, not a customer. The ratio matters: paying accounts are 2,150 / 14,300 = 15% of the headline figure, so the marketing number overstates the customer base by about 6.7x.

The deeper problem is one label serving two populations. Dashboards should name populations precisely — 'workspaces created (all time),' 'active paying accounts' — and ban unqualified nouns like 'customers' and 'users' from tiles. Most KPI disputes are not about arithmetic; they are about which population a friendly word is allowed to smuggle in.

A news site's dashboard tracks 'articles read per session,' up from 1.8 to 2.6 after a redesign. The redesign also split long articles into 3-page slideshows, each page counting as an 'article read.' Total time on site is flat. Did reading increase?

No measurable increase in reading occurred — the unit changed. One long article that used to count as 1 'read' now counts as up to 3 page-views labeled reads, so the metric can rise (1.8 to 2.6 is +44%) while total attention, the flat time-on-site, stays exactly the same. Readers are consuming the same content sliced thinner.

This is unit redefinition, the quiet cousin of the axis trick: nothing about the axis or definition banner changed, but the *thing being counted* did. When a metric jumps at a redesign, ask 'what is one unit of this metric now, and what was it before?' If the unit changed, the trend line across the seam is meaningless, however smooth it looks.

Our dashboard shows 'Support tickets resolved: 1,240 this week, up 15%.' I discover agents can now mark a ticket 'resolved' when they send any reply, whereas before it required customer confirmation. Confirmed resolutions actually fell from 1,080 to 990. Present the honest picture.

The honest picture is the opposite of the headline. Under the old definition the trend is 1,080 → 990, a fall of (1,080 - 990) / 1,080 = 8.3%. The dashboard's +15% (1,240 vs the old 1,080) compares this week's loose-definition count against last week's strict-definition count — a seam comparison again.

Worse, the new definition rewards the appearance of resolution: an agent reply that solves nothing now counts the same as a confirmed fix, so the metric will drift upward on its own as agents learn the incentive. Metrics that define success as an internal action ('we replied') rather than an external outcome ('the customer's problem is gone') reliably produce this pattern. Restore the confirmation requirement, or rename the tile to what it now measures: 'tickets answered.'

A marketplace dashboard shows 'GMV: $4.8M this month' as the hero number. GMV counts the full value of every transaction including cancelled orders ($310k) and fully refunded ones ($190k). Net transaction value is $4.3M. Is the hero number defensible?

As a labeled measure of gross throughput, barely; as the hero number, no. The cancellations and refunds are $500k — 10.4% of the claimed GMV — money that never settled to anyone. $4.8M - $0.31M - $0.19M = $4.3M is what actually moved.

GMV survives in dashboards because it is the largest available number and because marketplaces historically reported it. But decisions priced off GMV (take-rate revenue forecasts, growth claims) inherit the 10% phantom. The label discipline fixes most of it: if the tile said 'gross order value (incl. cancellations)' nobody would budget against it. Hero metrics should be the ones you would let an auditor read aloud.

Our internal dashboard reports 'Meeting hours per employee: 11.2 per week' as a productivity win, down from 13.5. But the calendar tool changed: recurring meetings that were declined by half the invitees no longer count. Attendance-adjusted, the old definition gives 12.9 for this week. How much of the win is real?

A minority of it. The reported drop is 13.5 → 11.2 = 2.3 hours. Restating this week under the old definition gives 12.9, so the real drop is 13.5 → 12.9 = 0.6 hours, and the definition change accounts for the other 1.7 hours — about 74% of the celebrated improvement.

This decomposition — restate the new period under the old rule — is the universal solvent for KPI jumps, and it should be standard practice whenever a measurement tool changes: dual-run or restate before announcing. A 0.6-hour real reduction may still be worth reporting. Reporting 2.3 is borrowing credit from a settings toggle.

A game studio's dashboard tracks 'DAU' but the number counts every app open, including push-notification dismissals that open the app for under a second. Product estimates true engaged DAU (session over 30 seconds) at 61,000 versus the dashboard's 148,000. What does this do to every other metric on the dashboard?

It poisons all of them, because DAU is the denominator of half the dashboard. Retention, ARPDAU (revenue per daily active user), conversion — each is computed per 'user,' and the user count is inflated by 148,000 / 61,000 = 2.43x. ARPDAU computed on the inflated base understates revenue per real user by the same factor; a funnel conversion of 5% on dashboard DAU is about 12% on engaged DAU.

Denominator definitions are load-bearing: corrupt the base population and every ratio built on it tilts. The fix is boring and total — define an engaged session (e.g., 30+ seconds or one meaningful action), restate the base, and let every dependent metric move to its true value at once. Dashboards rarely die from one wrong tile; they die from one wrong denominator under ten tiles.

Our growth chart shows weekly signups essentially flat: 1,610 last week, 1,600 this week (-0.6%). But the daily numbers this week were Mon 400, Tue 390, Wed 410, Thu 120, Fri 110, Sat 90, Sun 80. An engineer says something broke on Thursday. The growth lead says the week is fine. Who is right?

The engineer. The weekly total (400+390+410+120+110+90+80 = 1,600) is nearly identical to last week's 1,610, but it averages two different regimes: Mon-Wed averaged 400/day, Thu-Sun averaged 100/day — a collapse of 75% that began Thursday and persisted. The weekly sum hides it because the strong first three days compensate for the broken last four.

Aggregation over a window is a bet that the window contains one regime. When something breaks mid-window, totals lie politely. The operational fix is to chart daily values with the weekly total as an overlay, and to alert on run-rate (last 3 days vs prior 3 days), not on period totals. 'The week is fine' is true of the week and false of the business.

A factory's quality dashboard shows cumulative defects as a line that climbs steadily all year, and the plant manager is alarmed: 'defects keep rising.' Weekly defect counts were actually 90, 84, 70, 61, 48, 35, 22 over the last seven weeks. What is the cumulative chart really saying?

It is saying defects are positive numbers. A cumulative sum of any non-negative quantity can only rise or stay flat — it is structurally incapable of showing improvement. The weekly counts tell the real story: defects *fell* from 90 to 22 per week, a 76% improvement ((90-22)/90).

Cumulative charts are the right tool for budgets and totals-to-date ('have we hit the annual cap?'). For rates and flows — 'are we getting better?' — they are a trap, because their direction is predetermined by arithmetic rather than by the world. When a cumulative line worries someone, ask for the per-period values; the slope of the cumulative curve is the rate, and here the slope is visibly flattening, which is the improvement, drawn in code.

A nonprofit's annual report chart shows 'cumulative donors' rising smoothly from 2,000 to 5,400 over five years, presented as evidence of a 'growing, loyal donor base.' Donor counts per year (people who gave that year) were 2,000, 1,700, 1,450, 1,300, 1,250. What does the cumulative chart conceal?

It conceals a shrinking active base behind an ever-growing historical sum. Cumulative donors counts everyone who has *ever* given (2,000 + additions each year reaching 5,400), while the people who actually gave in each year fell every single year: 2,000 down to 1,250, a 37.5% decline. The organization is living off an accumulating past while its present contracts.

Cumulative series answer 'how much in total so far?' — useful for funds raised, useless for health. Any metric whose name contains 'cumulative' or 'all-time' should trigger the question: what does the per-period version look like? Loyalty would show up as stable or growing annual givers and a high repeat rate, neither of which this chart can express.

A slide compares two sales teams: 'Team A grew 50% this quarter; Team B grew only 10%.' Team A went from 2 deals to 3. Team B went from 200 deals to 220. The VP proposes moving budget from B to A. Do the percentages support that?

The percentages are accurate and the conclusion is backwards. Team A added 1 deal; Team B added 20. B's 'only 10%' is twenty times A's absolute growth, on a base one hundred times larger. Percentages erase the base, and with a base of 2, a single deal is 50% — noise dressed as performance.

Side-by-side percentages with wildly different denominators should always be shown with their counts: 'A: 2 → 3 deals (+50%); B: 200 → 220 deals (+10%).' Budget should follow absolute contribution and expected value, not the loudest ratio. A useful rule: never compare two percentages until you have seen both denominators; a percentage without its base is an advertisement, not a measurement.

A state health map colors counties by total flu cases: County X darkest with 900 cases, County Y pale with 300. County X has 3,000,000 residents; County Y has 300,000. The map's caption says 'X is the state's flu hotspot.' Compute the rates and verdict.

County X: 900 / 3,000,000 = 30 cases per 100,000 residents. County Y: 300 / 300,000 = 100 per 100,000. Per capita, Y's flu rate is 3.3 times X's. The map has it exactly backwards: X is darkest because it has ten times the people, and raw counts on a map mostly redraw the population map.

Choropleths must be colored by rates (cases per 100k) whenever the underlying populations differ — which is always. The counts are not useless (X needs more vaccine doses shipped; Y needs more intervention per person), but they answer logistics questions, not hotspot questions. Color by counts and every map of everything — crime, sales, disease — becomes the same map of where people live.

Our retail dashboard maps total sales by state and California dominates every quarter, which the team cites as 'our strongest market.' California has about 39M people; our per-capita sales there are $1.10 per resident, versus $3.40 in Colorado (population 5.8M). Total sales: CA $43M, CO $19.7M. What should 'strongest market' mean?

It depends on the decision, and the map only shows one candidate meaning. By totals, California is the biggest revenue pool ($43M vs $19.7M) — that matters for warehouse placement and absolute growth headroom. By intensity, Colorado is three times stronger per resident ($3.40 vs $1.10) — that matters for where the model works best and where expansion spending earns most per capita.

Check the per-capita figures: 43M / 39M = $1.10 ✓ and 19.7M / 5.8M = $3.40 ✓. The error is not the map but the caption: a totals map cannot testify about strength-as-affinity. Sophisticated dashboards show both layers — totals for scale decisions, rates for affinity decisions — and ban the unqualified word 'strongest' from map titles.

A/B test results: overall, variant B converts better (13.5%) than A (9.5%). But segmenting shows A beats B on mobile (9.0% vs 8.5%) AND on desktop (14.5% vs 14.0%). Traffic: A got 10,000 mobile and 1,000 desktop visitors; B got 1,000 mobile and 10,000 desktop. Explain the paradox with the actual counts.

Simpson's paradox, driven by the traffic mix. A's conversions: mobile 9.0% of 10,000 = 900; desktop 14.5% of 1,000 = 145; total 1,045 / 11,000 = 9.5%. B's: mobile 8.5% of 1,000 = 85; desktop 14.0% of 10,000 = 1,400; total 1,485 / 11,000 = 13.5%. A wins within each segment, but A was shown mostly to mobile visitors (the low-converting segment) while B was shown mostly to desktop — so B's overall average feasts on the better segment.

The overall rate is a weighted average where the weights (segment mix) differed between variants, so it compares mixes, not variants. Whenever an aggregate reverses every subgroup, suspect the weights. The fixes: randomize so mixes match, or compare within segments and standardize. An unsegmented dashboard number can be an average of the data and the allocation accident.

Our support dashboard shows 'average daily handle time this week: 514 minutes total across the team' — no wait, it shows average first-response time for the week as 514 ms for our status API: daily means were Mon 200, Tue 210, Wed 190, Thu 205, Fri 195, Sat 2,400, Sun 200 ms. The lead says 'weekly average is up, we're getting slower.' A junior says Saturday was an outage. Who is reading it right?

The junior. Six of the seven days sit at 190-210 ms — the system's normal state, median 200 ms. The weekly mean of (200+210+190+205+195+2,400+200)/7 = 3,600/7 = 514 ms is one catastrophic day averaged over six healthy ones. 'We're getting slower' describes a trend; the data describes an incident.

Means over windows containing outliers report the outlier's size divided by the window length — a number that describes neither the normal days nor the bad day (which was 2,400, not 514). Dashboards need the median for 'typical' and a separate incident view for 'worst.' Reporting 514 ms as the week's character misinforms in both directions: it makes normal look bad and the outage look mild.

A rolling 12-month average chart of our monthly revenue looks smooth and gently rising through June. Monthly revenue: Jul-Dec last year averaged $500k; this year Jan-Apr were $510k, $505k, $495k, $500k — then May was $310k and June $290k. Why does the rolling chart look calm?

Because each point of a 12-month rolling average contains ten months of the old regime. The May point averages last Jun-Apr (mostly ~$500k months) with May's $310k, diluting the collapse by a factor of twelve: the rolling value dips by roughly (500-310)/12 = about $16k instead of $190k. June dilutes two bad months. The line will take most of a year to 'notice' a change that has already happened.

Rolling averages trade responsiveness for smoothness — a legitimate trade for seasonal data, a dangerous one for regime detection. Pair them with the raw monthly series or a shorter window (3-month), and never let the smoothest available line be the only one on the dashboard. Smoothness is not the same as stability; sometimes it is just lag.

A chart compares two clinics by patient satisfaction: Clinic A 88% satisfied (88 of 100 patients), Clinic B 92% satisfied (46 of 50 patients). The bars show B clearly ahead and the regional manager wants to copy B's practices. What should temper that?

The denominators. B's 92% rests on 50 patients: each patient is worth 2 percentage points, so if just 3 of B's satisfied patients had answered differently, B would be at 86% — below A. A's 88% rests on 100 patients (1 point each) and is correspondingly steadier. The bars present both percentages with identical visual confidence, but one is built on half the evidence.

Percentages from different bases are not directly comparable until you ask how much each could wobble. Dashboards should print the n next to every percentage, and small-n percentages should be flagged or pooled over longer windows. '92% (n=50)' versus '88% (n=100)' is a much closer call than the bars suggest — possibly no real difference at all.

A city dashboard shows a choropleth of vaccinated residents by county, colored by count. The darkest county (210,000 vaccinated, population 300,000) is praised as the rollout leader; a pale county (95,000 vaccinated, population 100,000) is flagged for intervention. Check the rates.

Dark county: 210,000 / 300,000 = 70% vaccinated. Pale county: 95,000 / 100,000 = 95% vaccinated — nearly complete coverage. The 'leader' actually has 90,000 unvaccinated residents (30% of 300k) while the 'laggard' has only 5,000. The intervention resources are about to be sent to the county that needs them least.

Counts on maps measure size; rates measure performance. For a rollout, the performance metric is coverage (vaccinated / eligible population), and the logistics metric (doses to ship) is the unvaccinated *count* — note that even by that count, the dark county needs more (90,000 vs 5,000), so the map's conclusion fails on both readings. Before acting on any colored map, ask: is the color a count, a rate, or a density — and which one does my decision actually need?

Our dashboard's headline says 'Average order value: $48.' Store 1 averages $40 over 900 orders; Store 2 averages $120 over 100 orders. A regional VP computed the chain's AOV as (40 + 120) / 2 = $80 and asks why the dashboard disagrees with 'simple math.'

The dashboard is right and the VP averaged averages. True AOV is total revenue over total orders: Store 1 revenue = 900 x $40 = $36,000; Store 2 = 100 x $120 = $12,000; combined = $48,000 over 1,000 orders = $48.

The VP's $80 treats the two stores as equal contributors, but Store 1 has nine times the orders, so the pooled average must sit nine times closer to $40 than to $120: $48. Averages of group averages are only valid when group sizes are equal. Whenever you see a KPI computed by averaging other KPIs, check the weights — unweighted averages of averages are one of the most common silent errors in business dashboards.

A gym chain's dashboard shows 'average visits per member per month: 4.2, stable all year.' Membership doubled in January with a New Year cohort that visits 0.8 times a month, while the original members visit 6 times a month. Original members: 1,000. New cohort: 1,000, of whom many have already frozen. Why is 'stable at 4.2' suspicious, and what should be shown?

Do the weighted math: (1,000 x 6 + 1,000 x 0.8) / 2,000 = 6,800 / 2,000 = 3.4, not 4.2 — so either the mix or the visit rates differ from the story, and 'stable' is hiding *something*. The structural point stands regardless: a pooled average over a changing mix can stay flat while every segment moves, or move while every segment is flat. If the original cohort's visits slid from 6.0 to 5.2 while low-visit members churned out (raising their weight on the remainder)... the average can hold at any value.

Cohort the metric: visits per member split by join cohort, trended separately. Averages over populations whose composition is changing are stories about the composition as much as about behavior. 'Stable average, doubled membership' should always trigger the cohort view before anyone relaxes.

A chart shows 'percentage of revenue from subscriptions' for two business units side by side: Unit A 30%, Unit B 60%, with bars twice as tall for B and a caption 'B's subscription business is twice A's.' Unit A revenue is $10M; Unit B revenue is $2M. Compute the subscription dollars.

Unit A: 30% of $10M = $3.0M of subscription revenue. Unit B: 60% of $2M = $1.2M. A's subscription business is 2.5 times B's in dollars — the caption inverts reality. The bars compare shares of two very different wholes, and the eye reads them as amounts.

Percentages of different bases cannot be compared as magnitudes, full stop. The honest display pairs each share with its base: 'A: 30% of $10M = $3.0M; B: 60% of $2M = $1.2M,' or a stacked bar in dollars with the subscription segment labeled. Shares answer 'how is each unit composed?'; dollars answer 'how big is the business?' A chart that lets the first masquerade as the second will misdirect investment toward small, pure units and away from large, mixed ones.

Our marketing dashboard shows cost per acquisition by channel as bars: Search $42, Social $38, Podcast $55, Events $210. Events looks catastrophic. Events produced 12 customers last quarter; search produced 4,000. Total spend: Events $2,520, Search $168,000. What context changes the reading?

The events bar is an average over 12 outcomes: a single customer more or less swings it by about $16 (2,520 / 12 = $210; one more customer makes it 2,520 / 13 = $194). Search's $42 is averaged over 4,000 outcomes and barely moves with any single result. The chart presents both CPAs with the same visual certainty, but one is a stable rate and the other is a small-sample sketch.

That does not rescue events — $210 may genuinely be too expensive — but the decision differs: for search you are tuning a known rate; for events you are deciding whether to run more events to *learn* the rate. Small-denominator metrics should be displayed with their counts and treated as estimates with wide error bars, not as verdicts. A bar chart cannot show uncertainty, which is precisely why the counts must be printed on it.

A dashboard tile says 'Churn risk: average account health score 72/100, up from 70.' The portfolio: 90 small accounts averaging 74, and 10 enterprise accounts averaging 54 — enterprise is 60% of revenue. Last quarter enterprise averaged 61. What is the average hiding?

First, the pooled figure: (90 x 74 + 10 x 54) / 100 = (6,660 + 540) / 100 = 72 — arithmetically right, managerially wrong. The average rose because the numerous small accounts improved, while the 10 accounts carrying 60% of revenue deteriorated from 61 to 54. Weighted by revenue instead of by account count, the portfolio's health fell.

An unweighted average treats a $1k account and a $1M account as equal citizens. For risk, the weighting should follow the exposure: revenue-weighted health is the number that predicts next quarter's income. The general pattern — average improves, weighted reality worsens — recurs wherever a few big units matter more than many small ones: key accounts, large servers, major routes. Ask of every average: averaged over what, weighted by what, and who is invisible inside it?

A weather-style chart in our ops review shows monthly average temperature at our warehouse: June average 24°C, and the presenter concludes 'no heat risk to the stored product in June; the limit is 30°C.' Daily highs in June included six days above 34°C, with a peak of 38°C. The product degrades after 4 hours above 30°C. Verdict?

The average is answering the wrong question. Heat damage is driven by *excursions above a threshold*, and a monthly mean of 24°C is fully compatible with six days above 34°C — cool nights and mild days pull the mean down while the product cooks in the afternoons. The relevant statistics are hours above 30°C and the daily maximum, not the mean.

This is the general failure of averages for threshold phenomena: flood risk lives in peak river height, not average flow; server risk lives in peak load, not average load; safety lives in the tail. When damage is nonlinear — fine below a line, bad above it — the dashboard must show exceedances (count and duration above the threshold) and maxima. A mean can certify comfort while the tails do the damage.

A sales chart shows Q1-Q4 revenue as four bars: 100, 110, 121, 133 (in $k) titled 'Growth accelerating!' The growth rates are 10%, 10%, 10%. Then a second chart from the same data plots the *cumulative* revenue: 100, 210, 331, 464, with bars getting dramatically taller and taller gaps. Why does the cumulative version look like acceleration?

Because cumulative bars grow by construction: each bar contains all previous quarters, so heights must increase, and the *increments* between cumulative bars grow in dollars (110, 121, 133) even at a constant percentage growth rate — constant-ratio growth produces expanding absolute steps. The cumulative chart converts steady 10% compounding into a visual of runaway acceleration.

Compounding is genuinely powerful, but the honest pictures are the per-quarter bars (100, 110, 121, 133) or the growth-rate line (flat at 10%). Cumulative displays answer 'how much in total so far' — for a revenue-to-date target they are fine. For judging momentum they double-count every past success into every future bar. When a chart's bars can only grow, its message was decided before the data arrived.

An HR dashboard shows 'average employee tenure: 5.8 years, rising steadily' as evidence that retention is improving.
