The company hired nobody for two years during a freeze, and layoffs last year removed mostly employees with under 2 years' tenure. Why can average tenure rise while retention is unchanged or worse?

Average tenure is a property of who is *currently employed*, and it rises mechanically whenever time passes without junior hires: every surviving employee ages one year per year, and with no new starters diluting the pool, the average climbs on its own. Removing short-tenure employees in layoffs raises it further — the average improved *because* people left, the opposite of retention.

This is survivorship in a dashboard tile: the metric describes the survivors, and exits (the retention failures) vanish from it. Real retention measurement follows cohorts: of the people who started in 2023, what fraction remain? A rising average tenure alongside a hiring freeze is arithmetic, not loyalty, and presenting it as a retention win rewards the freeze itself.

A chart in a city budget presentation shows police spending per capita for two cities as bars of nearly equal height: City A $310 per resident, City B $298. Below, a second chart shows total spending: A $62M, B $298M. A resident says the cities 'spend about the same on policing.' Untangle the two claims.

Both charts are honest; they answer different questions and the resident has merged them. Per capita, the cities are indeed close: $310 vs $298 per resident (about 4% apart) — that is the right lens for 'how much policing does each resident fund/experience.' In total, B spends 298 / 62 = 4.8 times A, because B has about five times the population (B: 298M / 298 = 1,000,000 residents; A: 62M / 310 = 200,000) — the right lens for budget scale and purchasing.

Confusion between rates and totals is the most common citizen-level chart error, and presentations exploit it by choosing whichever flatters the argument. The discipline is to state, for every comparison, whether the claim is about intensity (per capita) or scale (total) — and to be suspicious when a speaker switches lenses mid-argument.

Redesign this honestly: a vendor's bar chart of defect rates for four factories — 4.1%, 4.4%, 4.6%, 5.9% — with the y-axis starting at 4%, making the worst factory's bar look dramatically taller than the best one's. Same data, fair picture. What do you draw, and what does it cost?

Draw bars from zero with the values labeled on top: 4.1, 4.4, 4.6, 5.9. On a zero baseline the bars stand in true proportion — the worst factory's bar is 5.9 / 4.1 = 1.44 times the best one's height, not the ~5x the truncated version showed (visible lengths above 4% were 0.1 vs 1.9, a 19x ratio, in fact).

What the honest version reveals: three factories clustered tightly (4.1-4.6) and one genuine outlier at 5.9 — a real, actionable story, just a quieter one. What it costs: drama. A 44% higher defect rate is worth a quality program, not a panic, and the chart now says exactly that. If the differences feel too small to see at zero baseline, that feeling *is* the data: switch to a dot plot on a labeled 3.5-6.5% scale, where position (not length) carries the value and zooming is legitimate.

Redesign honestly: a dual-axis slide plotting marketing spend (left axis) and revenue (right axis) with the axes tuned so the lines overlap, implying spend drives revenue one-for-one. The actual data, six months: spend $20k, $25k, $22k, $30k, $28k, $35k; revenue $400k, $420k, $415k, $460k, $450k, $470k. What do you show instead?

Show two stacked panels sharing one x-axis (months), each series on its own honestly labeled scale — or better, show the derived quantity the claim is about: revenue per marketing dollar by month: 20.0, 16.8, 18.9, 15.3, 16.1, 13.4. That series *falls* over the period: spend rose 75% (20k to 35k) while revenue rose 17.5% (400k to 470k), so each dollar is returning less.

The overlapping-lines version hid the single most decision-relevant fact in the data. Two panels cost the slide its pretty synchronicity; what they buy is that nobody can tune an axis to manufacture agreement. When a chart's job is to argue that X drives Y, plot the ratio or the scatter (spend on x, revenue on y) — forms where the relationship, or its absence, cannot be faked by scaling.

Redesign honestly: a 14-slice pie of support ticket categories (shares from 19% down to 1%, with the top four at 19, 16, 14, 12 and ten slices between 1% and 6%). The team needs to decide where to add help docs. What replaces the pie?

A sorted horizontal bar chart of all 14 categories, values labeled, with a cumulative line or annotation if useful: the top four categories sum to 19+16+14+12 = 61% of tickets, so the chart should make that concentration obvious — four long bars, then a tail. Sorted bars turn 'where do we write help docs?' into a reading exercise: start at the top, work down until the marginal category is worth less than the effort.

The pie forced readers to match 14 legend colors to 14 similar wedges and estimate angles; the bar chart replaces estimation with length comparison along one baseline, the most accurate judgment the eye makes. What it costs: the 'share of a whole' gestalt — which the cumulative annotation restores ('top 4 = 61% of all tickets'). Nothing decision-relevant is lost; the squinting is.

Redesign honestly: an investor update shows cumulative registered users climbing from 100k to 900k over three years as the sole growth chart. Monthly new registrations were 40k in year 1, 25k in year 2, 15k in year 3 (monthly averages), and monthly actives fell over the same period. What should the slide show?

Show the flows, not the stock: monthly new registrations as bars (averaging 40k, then 25k, then 15k a month — acquisition is decelerating, down 62.5% from year 1 to year 3) and monthly active users as a line on the same time axis. The cumulative curve (which sums to the 900k) can stay as a faint context line if the audience needs scale, labeled 'all-time registrations.'

The original slide's curve could only rise — even in the worst month, registrations add something — so it certified growth in a period when both acquisition and activity were shrinking. Honest cost: the slide now shows a business with a growth problem, which is presumably why the cumulative version was chosen. But investors price honesty eventually; better the chart shows the problem while it is still fixable.

Redesign honestly: a latency dashboard whose hero tile is 'Average response time: 240 ms' while p95 is 1,900 ms and support tickets about slowness keep rising. What does the redesigned tile row look like?

Replace the single mean with the distribution's landmarks: p50 120 ms, p95 1,900 ms, p99 4,200 ms, plus a small histogram or a 'requests over 2s today: 8,400' counter. The mean can live in a secondary row for capacity planning, where it belongs.

The redesign reveals what the mean concealed: half of requests are fast (p50 120 ms — the typical experience is fine), but 1 in 20 waits nearly 2 seconds and roughly 1 in 100 waits over 4. The support tickets were never mysterious; they were the p95 population introducing itself. Cost of honesty: three numbers where one sat before, and a hero tile that can get worse in public. That is the point — a tile that cannot embarrass anyone cannot warn anyone either.

Redesign honestly: a choropleth of flu cases by county colored with raw counts (largest county darkest at 900 cases, 3M residents; a small county pale at 300 cases, 300k residents). A public-health team will allocate mobile clinics from this map. What do you hand them instead?

Hand them a rate map — cases per 100,000 residents: the big county is 30 per 100k, the small one is 100 per 100k — with the counts printed inside each county as labels. The color now shows intensity (where the disease is most concentrated), and the labels preserve the logistics (where the most patients are).

The allocation flips: mobile clinics go first to the pale county on the old map, which has 3.3x the infection rate. What the redesign costs: the comforting match between dark color and 'big place with many cases' intuition, plus one extra legend line explaining the rate. What it buys: resources aimed by need per person rather than by population size. For any map that drives allocation, color = rate, labels = counts, no exceptions.

Redesign honestly: a funnel graphic whose stage widths were drawn by eye (100%, 75%, 55%, 50%) for actual stages Visits 100,000 → Signups 40,000 → Trials 30,000 → Paid 25,000. The growth team wants to know where to work. What does the honest version show?

Widths proportional to the counts: 100%, 40%, 30%, 25% — and beside each transition, its conversion rate: visit→signup 40%, signup→trial 75%, trial→paid 83%. The honest funnel has a cliff at the top and gentle steps after, the exact opposite silhouette from the drawn version.

That silhouette is the strategy: the leak is visit→signup, where 60,000 of 100,000 visitors vanish; improving trial→paid from 83% to 90% would add only about 2,100 paid users (30,000 x 0.07), while lifting visit→signup from 40% to 45% adds 5,000 signups that flow down at current rates (5,000 x 75% x 83% = about +3,100 paid). The eye-drawn funnel sent the team to polish the healthiest stage. Cost of honesty: the funnel looks broken. It is — that is the information.

Redesign honestly: a line chart of satisfaction by department (HR 3.9, Sales 4.2, Operations 3.6, Legal 4.0, Support 3.8) with dramatic zigzags and a narrative about 'the Operations plunge.' Same data, honest picture — and what happens to the narrative?

Draw five bars, sorted descending: Sales 4.2, Legal 4.0, HR 3.9, Support 3.8, Operations 3.6 — with the scale running 0-5 (or a dot plot on a labeled 3-4.5 scale if the small differences matter) and the company average (3.9) marked as a reference line.

The narrative dies, correctly: there is no plunge or recovery because there is no path between departments; there is a 0.6-point spread between best and worst on a 5-point scale, with Operations modestly below average. The honest chart's story is 'departments differ a little; Operations is worth a conversation, not an intervention.' Cost: the deck loses its drama arc. Gain: nobody launches a turnaround program at a rounding difference. When removing the chart-type artifact removes the story, the story was the artifact.

Redesign honestly: a quarterly business review slide showing revenue as a cumulative year-to-date line that rises beautifully to $4.2M by Q4, while quarterly revenue actually went $1.3M, $1.15M, $0.95M, $0.8M. What belongs on the slide?

Bars for the quarters themselves — 1.3, 1.15, 0.95, 0.8 — which show a business shrinking every quarter: Q4 is (1.3 - 0.8) / 1.3 = 38% below Q1. The cumulative line may stay as a thin secondary line if the audience tracks a full-year target ($4.2M against, say, a $5M goal — which reframes the cumulative number as an 84% attainment, not a triumph).

The original slide committed the cumulative fallacy in its purest form: a sum of positive quarters rises even while the business contracts, so the chart's direction was guaranteed in January. The redesign costs the presenter the rising line and buys the only question that matters — why is each quarter smaller than the last, and what changes that? A chart whose shape is predetermined by its type is not reporting; it is wallpaper.

Redesign honestly: a before/after slide for a pricing change. Before: bars show monthly revenue for the 3 months pre-change (axis from zero, bars to $210k, $215k, $205k). After: the 3 months post-change are drawn on a *different chart* with its axis starting at $180k (bars to $225k, $230k, $228k) and the caption 'revenue surges after pricing change.' One chart, honest scales — what does it show?

One panel, one axis from zero, six bars: 210, 215, 205, 225, 230, 228. Pre-change average: (210+215+205)/3 = $210k. Post-change average: (225+230+228)/3 = $227.7k. The honest claim is 'revenue up about 8.4% on average after the change' — a solid, defensible result.

The two-chart version committed two sins: incomparable scales (the after-chart's zoom made ~$20k differences tower) and the word 'surges' for an 8% effect. Side-by-side charts with different axes are the print version of the dual-axis trick. Cost of the single chart: the increase looks modest, because it is modest. Gain: the claim survives the first skeptical question, which in a pricing review is the whole game.

In a meeting, a vendor shows a conversion chart: 'Conversion up from 2.4% to 3.75% since our tool launched — a 56% improvement.' Over the same period our traffic shifted from 80% mobile / 20% desktop to 50/50. Mobile converts at 1.5% and desktop at 6%, and neither segment's rate has changed. You get one question. Which one, and what does it reveal?

Ask: 'What are the conversion rates by device, before and after?' — the mix question. Now do the blend arithmetic the chart skipped. Before: 0.8 x 1.5% + 0.2 x 6% = 1.2 + 1.2 = 2.4%. After: 0.5 x 1.5% + 0.5 x 6% = 0.75 + 3.0 = 3.75%. The entire 'improvement' is reproduced exactly by the traffic shift alone, with both segment rates frozen — desktop converts four times better than mobile, and the audience simply became more desktop-heavy.

The vendor's tool may have helped, hurt, or done nothing; the blended chart cannot say, because an aggregate rate is a weighted average and the weights moved. In meetings, the mix question ('did the composition change?') dissolves more miracle charts than any other, because aggregates inherit every shift in who showed up.

A department head presents bars showing her team's output 'up 40%' after a reorganization: the before bar is 50 tickets/week, the after bar is 70. A colleague whispers that the chart's axis starts at 30. You get one question in the meeting. Which, and does the claim survive it?

Ask: 'Does that axis start at zero — and can we see the bars from zero?' The claim itself is arithmetically true: (70 - 50) / 50 = 40%. But the visual is not: above a 30 floor, the visible bar lengths are 20 and 40, so the after bar looks twice the before bar — a 100% visual for a 40% fact.

Whether the claim 'survives' depends on its use: as a sentence ('output rose 40%, from 50 to 70 tickets a week') it is fine; as a picture it overstates by design. The meeting habit to build: for any bar chart, your eyes go to the axis floor before the bar tops. It takes one second, and it converts most dramatic bar charts into their true, quieter selves — after which the real discussion (was the reorg the cause? what about ticket complexity?) can start.

In a QBR, the 'active customers' line rises smoothly from 8,100 to 9,300 across the year with no visible seam. You remember the CRM migration in June reclassified trial accounts as customers. What is your one question, and what answer would satisfy you?

Ask: 'Was this series restated under the current definition for the months before June — and if not, where is the break?' A smooth line across a known definition change is the tell: real spliced series usually show a step at the seam, so smoothness suggests either a proper restatement (good) or a quiet backfill of the new definition into old months without documentation (unauditable), or worst, that the rise *is* the reclassification — 1,200 trial accounts would exactly explain 8,100 → 9,300.

The satisfying answer is a number: 'June restated under both definitions: 8,640 old, 9,050 new; the year's real growth is X.' Without a dual-run at the seam, nobody in the room knows the growth rate, including the presenter. Definition changes are the only chart events that can manufacture growth from nothing, so they get the first question.

A startup founder shows a beautiful upward line: 'Revenue, last 8 quarters,' values rising from $90k to $310k. You notice the y-axis is unlabeled and the line is smooth — suspiciously smooth for a young company. What are your two quick questions before admiring it?

First: 'Is this quarterly revenue, or cumulative?' Cumulative revenue over 8 quarters would rise smoothly and inevitably; a final cumulative value of $310k across two years is a very different business from $310k *per quarter*. Second: 'What are the actual quarterly values?' — read them off and check the shape: real young-company revenue is lumpy (a lost client dents it), so a perfectly smooth curve often means cumulative data, a forecast blended into actuals, or a trend line drawn instead of the data.

Neither question accuses anyone of anything; both are about what the line *is*. A chart that cannot survive 'what exactly is plotted, and what are the numbers?' was never evidence — it was decoration with an axis. Admire after the answers, not before.

A manager presents a map of customer complaints by store district, dark red over the downtown district (1,400 complaints), pale over the suburbs (350). She proposes moving the entire quality team downtown. Store counts: downtown has 14 stores doing 92,000 transactions a month; suburbs have 3 stores doing 18,000. Give her the two numbers that should precede any move.

Complaints per 1,000 transactions: downtown 1,400 / 92,000 = 15.2 per 1,000; suburbs 350 / 18,000 = 19.4 per 1,000. Per transaction, the suburbs complain *more* — the downtown darkness is mostly volume: more stores, more transactions, more complaints, at a lower rate.

That does not settle the staffing question by itself — downtown still holds 1,400 of the 1,750 total complaints (80%), so a volume-based argument for downtown staff exists. But the map as presented argues 'downtown is where the problem is worst,' and by rate that is false; if the quality team's job is fixing the worst *rate*, it goes to the suburbs. Rate for diagnosis, count for logistics — and a map that shows only counts will always send you to the biggest place, whatever the question was.

A slide in a board meeting shows a single dramatic number-chart pair: 'Customer acquisition cost: $96 → $61' with a steep downward line, credited to a new agency. You learn the earlier period's CAC included brand advertising spend and the later one excludes it. What is the state of the claim?

Unknowable as presented — the two numbers were computed under different definitions, so the $35 drop (36%) is some unknown blend of real improvement and reclassification. If brand spend was, say, $30 of the original $96, the like-for-like comparison might be $66 → $61, a 7.6% improvement — still fine, but a different agency review.

The board-meeting move is not to accuse but to pin: 'Can we get both periods under one definition by Friday?' Until then the claim is on hold, and any decision riding on it (renewing the agency at a higher retainer) should be too. The pattern to internalize: a metric improvement that coincides with a measurement change is presumed to *be* the measurement change until a restated series proves otherwise. That single presumption, applied consistently, kills most dashboard miracles.
